learning_objective: 🎯 Learn how to measure the total wealth and income of a nation using circular flow, GDP, and various national accounting methods!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: In a simplified economy, households provide factors of production (land, labor, capital) to firms, and firms give back factor payments (rent, wages, interest). Households then spend this money on goods and services produced by the firms, creating a continuous loop.

You can calculate National Income in three ways: Product/Value Added Method (sum of all value added), Income Method (sum of all factor payments), and Expenditure Method (sum of all final expenditures). They all yield the exact same result!

Nominal GDP is calculated using current year prices, so it can look big just because of inflation. Real GDP is calculated using constant base-year prices, showing the actual growth in physical output.

Higher GDP doesn't always mean people are happier. It ignores the distribution of income (rich getting richer), non-monetary exchanges (like a parent cooking dinner), and negative externalities (like factory pollution).

fun_activity.title: 💵 Follow the ₹100 Note
fun_activity.instructions: Track a ₹100 note! A farmer uses it to buy clothes from a tailor (Expenditure). The tailor uses it to pay his assistant's wages (Income). The assistant buys wheat from the farmer (Value added). The single ₹100 note creates continuous economic activity in the circular flow!

exam_tips: 📌 Always subtract 'Intermediate Consumption' from Value of Output to get Value Added, otherwise you make the mistake of double counting.
📌 To convert Gross to Net, subtract Depreciation. To convert Market Price (MP) to Factor Cost (FC), subtract Net Indirect Taxes (Taxes - Subsidies).
📌 Learn the externalities concept well; it is frequently asked to explain why GDP is not a perfect index of welfare.
quick_recap: ⭐ The sum of Value Added by all firms in an economy gives the Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
⭐ NNP at factor cost is officially recognized as the 'National Income' of a country.
⭐ Double counting inflates the GDP, which is avoided by using the Value Added method or counting only final goods.
